A higher log level changes text severity but leaves the span successful, so failure-rate queries, alerts, and dashboards still see nothing wrong. It only helps if a human happens to be reading logs, which is the workflow that already failed for two days.

A custom metric is a reasonable supplementary signal, but reviewing it weekly guarantees a multi-day detection gap — the same gap the team just experienced. It also leaves the span status wrong, so the primary failure signals remain misleading.
principle: mark the span as failed even when the request degrades gracefully
relatedConcept: Span status and recorded exceptions are the structured failure signals that alerts and failure-rate queries consume; swallowed exceptions make healthy dashboards lie.
overallExplanation: Record the exception on the span and set span status to error while still returning the partial result, so failure-rate queries and alerts see it. Log-level changes leave the span successful, and re-raising trades observability for an outage.

question: After a release at 14:05, users report the retrieval API feels slower, but overall average duration moved from 620 ms to 690 ms and nobody is convinced. An engineer wants a chart that would settle whether tail latency changed at the release boundary. Which query is most useful?
options: requests | where timestamp between (ago(3h) .. now()) | summarize percentiles(duration, 50, 95, 99) by bin(timestamp, 5m) | render timechart
requests | where timestamp > ago(3h) | summarize avg(duration) by bin(timestamp, 1h) | render timechart
requests | where timestamp > ago(3h) | summarize count() by bin(timestamp, 5m) | render timechart
requests | where timestamp > ago(3h) and duration > 2000 | project timestamp, name, duration | order by duration desc
optionExplanations: Correct. The dispute is about tail latency, which averages hide, so the chart needs percentiles — and it needs enough time resolution to show a step at 14:05 rather than smearing it. Percentiles per five-minute bucket rendered as a time series makes a p95 or p99 shift at the release boundary immediately visible.

Hourly averages are the worst possible resolution for this question: a change at 14:05 is diluted across the 14:00 bucket, and the average is the statistic that already failed to convince anyone. It reproduces the ambiguity the engineer is trying to resolve.
Request counts describe traffic volume, not latency. A throughput chart is worth having alongside a latency chart, but on its own it cannot say whether requests got slower.

Listing individual slow requests shows examples without showing whether their rate or magnitude changed at the boundary. There is no time series and no baseline, so it cannot distinguish a new problem from slow requests that always existed.
principle: compare percentiles over time buckets to see a latency shift
relatedConcept: Averages mask tail regressions, so release comparisons rely on percentile time series at a resolution fine enough to expose the change point.
overallExplanation: Chart percentiles(duration, 50, 95, 99) by bin(timestamp, 5m) as a timechart so a tail-latency step at the release boundary is visible. Hourly averages smear the change, counts measure traffic, and sample rows offer no baseline.

question: A downstream scoring service is saturated: its p95 latency has risen from 300 ms to 9 s, it returns 503 for about 40 percent of calls, and the caller's Service Bus backlog is growing. Retries with backoff and jitter are already in place, and adding attempts has made things worse. What should the caller add?
options: A circuit breaker that opens after a failure threshold, fails fast while open, and probes with a limited number of trial calls before closing again
A larger connection pool so more requests can be in flight and fewer wait for a connection
A longer per-attempt timeout so slow-but-eventually-successful calls are not abandoned prematurely
More consumer instances so the growing backlog is drained faster
optionExplanations: Correct. Once a dependency is saturated, correctly spaced retries still add load, so the caller needs to stop sending for a while. A circuit breaker does exactly that: it opens on a failure threshold, fails fast so callers are not blocked for nine seconds, and probes with a small number of trial calls so it can close again once health returns — giving the dependency room to recover.

A larger pool lets the caller push more concurrent requests at a service that is already failing 40 percent of them, which deepens the saturation. It is the right fix when the caller is connection-starved and the dependency is healthy, which is the opposite of this situation.

Longer timeouts mean each doomed call occupies a worker and a concurrency slot for longer, so throughput falls and the backlog grows faster. It also increases the load the dependency must carry concurrently, which is what saturation is.

Scaling consumers multiplies the request rate against the saturated dependency, so the failure rate rises and the backlog keeps growing. Adding consumer capacity only helps when the constraint is consumer-side, and here every signal points downstream.
principle: when a dependency is saturated, shed load rather than push harder
relatedConcept: Circuit breaking complements retry: retry handles isolated transient faults, while breaking handles a dependency that needs relief to recover.
overallExplanation: Add a circuit breaker that opens on a failure threshold, fails fast, and probes before closing, so the saturated dependency gets relief. Bigger pools, longer timeouts, and more consumers all increase pressure on the stage that is already the constraint.

question: Before a performance review an engineer must show where the service's time actually goes: which dependency targets consume the largest share of total time across all requests in the last day, not merely which individual calls were slowest. Which aggregation answers that question?
options: dependencies | where timestamp > ago(1d) | summarize total = sum(duration), calls = count() by target | order by total desc
dependencies | where timestamp > ago(1d) | summarize max(duration) by target | order by max_duration desc
dependencies | where timestamp > ago(1d) | top 100 by duration desc | project target, duration
dependencies | where timestamp > ago(1d) | summarize dcount(operation_Id) by target | order by dcount_operation_Id desc
optionExplanations: Correct. Share of total time is frequency multiplied by duration, which is exactly what sum(duration) per target computes, and carrying count() alongside shows whether a target dominates because it is slow or because it is called constantly. That distinction is what turns the chart into an actionable optimization list.

The maximum surfaces the single worst call per target, which is dominated by outliers and says nothing about aggregate cost. A target with one pathological 30-second call can outrank one consuming hours of cumulative time.

A top-100 listing shows the slowest individual calls, which is the comparison the engineer explicitly wants to move beyond. A dependency called two million times at 40 ms each never appears in that list yet may be the largest consumer of time in the service.

Counting distinct operations per target measures how many requests touch a dependency, which is a useful reach metric but not a time metric. A target touched by every request could still contribute a negligible share of total duration.
principle: total time is frequency times duration, so sum before you rank
relatedConcept: Aggregate cost analysis ranks by summed duration rather than by peak duration, which is how frequently-called fast dependencies get their due weight.
overallExplanation: Rank by sum(duration) per target with count() alongside so both slow calls and very frequent ones are weighted correctly. Maximums and top-N listings surface outliers, and distinct counts measure reach rather than time.

question: A synchronous endpoint must answer within 5 seconds or an upstream gateway abandons the connection. Its model call has a 10-second per-attempt timeout and retries up to three times with backoff, so a failing request can occupy about 35 seconds. Traces show requests still running long after the gateway gave up. How should the timeout design change?
options: Set an overall deadline below the gateway's 5 seconds and derive per-attempt timeouts and the attempt count from the time remaining in that budget
Raise the gateway's timeout to 40 seconds so the endpoint's existing retry sequence can complete
Keep the timeouts as they are but cancel the retries when the client disconnects, since a disconnected client no longer needs the result
Reduce the per-attempt timeout to 5 seconds so no single attempt can exceed the gateway's limit
optionExplanations: Correct. Timeouts must be budgeted from the outside in: the caller's deadline is the constraint, and everything inside — attempt timeouts, backoff waits, and how many attempts are even worth starting — has to fit inside what remains of it. Deriving inner timeouts from the remaining budget also means the last attempt is never started when there is no time for it to finish.

Stretching the upstream contract to accommodate an internal retry policy imposes a 40-second worst case on every caller, which for a synchronous endpoint is indistinguishable from a hang. It also inverts the dependency: internal implementation detail should fit the published latency contract, not redefine it.

Cancelling on disconnect is genuinely worth doing to reclaim capacity, but it is a mitigation rather than a fix: the request still consumes resources up to the moment of disconnection, and the endpoint still has no design that lets it answer within its own contract. The budget violation remains.

Equal per-attempt and overall limits leave no room for backoff waits or for a second attempt, so the first slow call consumes the entire budget and the retry policy becomes decorative. A per-attempt timeout must be a fraction of the overall deadline for retries to mean anything.
principle: budget timeouts from the caller's deadline inward
relatedConcept: Retries multiply latency, so per-attempt timeouts and attempt counts are only correct relative to an overall deadline inherited from the caller.
overallExplanation: Set an overall deadline inside the gateway's 5 seconds and derive per-attempt timeouts and attempt counts from the time remaining. Raising the upstream timeout hides the design flaw, and equal inner and outer timeouts leave no room for retries.
